attributes.title: Level 10

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you test out the project by moving the Player sprite around the tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite moves around the tilemap?

❓ What do you notice about the size of the tilemap during game play?

❓ What might be added to improve the User Experience (UX) of this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In this activity, the ninja will explore adding the Minimap extension to the project. The Minimap extension creates a smaller representation of the existing tilemap, which can be useful for identifying other sprites, collectibles, and obstacles on a large tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Begin by exploring the existing project!


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap on screen. Use the direction buttons to move the Player sprite around the screen, then notice what happens when it overlaps the Enemy or Food sprite.


Notice that the tilemap is larger than the size of the screen, which makes it hard to tell where the different sprites are!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the minimap’s border to a complementary color, so that it clearly stands out on the tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the minimap function do? Why might it be useful in a project?

❓ What might the minimap’s border width and color parameters be set to, so that the image is clearly visible against the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The minimap function creates a minimap image, which is a smaller representation of the existing tilemap. This can be useful for identifying sprites and obstacles on a large tilemap. In order for a minimap to be generated, a tilemap must be created first. 

💡 The minimap function only creates a minimap image. In order for the minimap to be visible on screen, a sprite must be created with its image set to the minimap.

💡 Prompt the ninja to either play the project, or look at the tilemap in the Assets menu, to identify what color to use for the minimap’s border.
steps.instructions:
Use the Minimap extension to keep track of sprite’s locations on the tilemap!


Click Extensions then scroll down to add the arcade-minimap extension to the project.


Below the code that creates the Food sprite, add a // minimap set up comment. 


Open Minimap and drag [minimap] underneath. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


let myMinimap = minimap.minimap()

The minimap function creates a minimap image, which is a smaller representation of the existing tilemap. It takes 3 parameters: scale, borderWidth, and borderColor.


Inside the parentheses, type MinimapScale and a dot operator, then select Eighth from the code completion tool. This will set the minimap’s size to an eighth of the original tilemap’s size. Then, set the borderWidth and borderColor parameters by typing 2 numbers, separated by commas. These can be updated once the minimap appears on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the minimap’s border width and color parameters, so that it stands out against the tilemap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the mapSprite’s x and y coordinates be set to, so that the image appears in the top left corner of the screen?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite moves to a different location on the tilemap? Is the minimap still visible?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the tilemap is larger than the size of the screen. Because the camera is set on the Player sprite, if the Player sprite moves away from the top left corner of the tilemap, the minimap will no longer be visible. In the next step, a sprite flag will be used to make the minimap remain fixed on screen. 

💡 Now that the minimap is visible on screen, encourage the ninja to tinker with the border width and color parameters, so that the image stands out against the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Display the minimap’s image on screen!


Create a mapSprite underneath the code that created the minimap image to display the minimap. Set the sprite’s image parameter by typing myMinimap and a dot operator, then selecting image from the code completion tool.   


Underneath, set the mapSprite’s position so that it appears in the top left corner of the screen. The mapSprite will be centered on the x and y coordinates.


Click ▶ to see the minimap in the top left corner of the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the setFlag functions on parameter to true?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where does the minimap appear when the Player sprite moves around the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the RelativeToCamera flag draws a sprite on a position relative to the camera. It’s useful for drawing User Interface (UI) elements (such as score/life variables, text, etc.) to the screen that remain in a fixed position, even when the camera moves.
steps.instructions:
Use a sprite flag to pin the minimap’s position, so that it’s always visible on screen.


Notice that the camera is already set to follow the Player sprite. 


Open Sprites, then drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the mapSprite’s code. Update the sprite’s name, then replace AutoDestroy with RelativeToCamera from the code completion tool and update the on parameter, so that the mapSprite has a fixed position on screen and will not move when the camera does. 


Click ▶ to see the minimap in the top left corner of the screen, regardless of the Player sprite’s position on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you test out the Player sprite’s scale on the minimap, then update the parameter accordingly?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does showing the Player Sprite's location on the minimap image improve the User Experience (UX)?

❓ What might the Player sprite’s scale be set to, so that it is clearly visible on the minimap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that because the tilemap is larger than the size of the screen, the minimap can be useful for identifying where sprites and obstacles are located to inform a sprite’s movement. 

💡 Have the ninja consider what the Player sprite’s scale should be set to. Prompt the ninja to think about whether it should be smaller than, larger than, or the same as its original size. If the ninja is unfamiliar with decimals, explain the concept to them in thinking about whether the sprite should be displayed as half or a quarter of its original size and what number that converts to.
steps.instructions:
Add the Player sprite to the minimap to track its movement on screen!


Open Minimap and drag [draw (mySprite) on (myMinimap)] under the mapSprite’s code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

minimap.includeSprite(myMinimap, mySprite)

The includeSprite function draws a sprite onto a minimap image. It takes 3 parameters: minimap, sprite, and spriteScale. 


Set the sprite parameter to the Player sprite, then type a comma and a number to set the spriteScale parameter. Use a decimal number to set the Player sprite’s scale to less than its original size.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite appear on the minimap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the getImage function inside the parentheses of the setImage function, to update the minimap’s image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should let be deleted from the minimap function inside the onUpdate loop?

❓ What should the mapSprite’s image be set to?

❓ Why does the minimap code need to be placed inside an onUpdate loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the let keyword declares a new variable. Since the ninja has already created a minimap image, the image does not need to be declared, just updated. Because the minimap function was declared outside of the onUpdate loop, it can be accessed throughout the project, including inside of the loop. 

💡 Point out to the ninja that the default parameter for the getImage function also creates a new minimap image. Because the ninja should update the existing minimap image, the default parameter code should be deleted and replaced with myMinimap to update the existing image.

💡 The minimap code should be placed inside an onUpdate loop so that when the Player sprite moves around the tilemap, the minimap image is constantly reset with the Player sprite’s new location as the game updates.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite’s position doesn’t update as it moves around the tilemap.


Add an onUpdate loop underneath // minimap set up. Copy the minimap function and paste it inside the loop. Delete the keyword let from the minimap function, so that the existing minimap’s image is updated. Then, cut the includeSprite function and paste it inside the loop.


Below, add code to set the mapSprite’s image. Delete img` `, then open Minimap and drag [minimap (image)] inside the parentheses. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

minimap.getImage(let myMinimap = minimap.minimap())

The getImage function retrieves a new minimap’s image. Replace the code inside the parentheses with myMinimap to set the mapSprite’s image to the current minimap.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite’s position update on the minimap as it moves around the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you tinker with the scale parameter in the includeSprite functions so that the sprites are clearly visible on the minimap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is displayed on the tilemap while the Player and Enemy sprites move around the tilemap?

❓ What might the Enemy and Food sprites’ scales be set to?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Now, when the sprites move around the tilemap, the minimap image is reset with the Player, Enemy, and Food sprites’ locations to inform the user’s strategy.

💡 Have the ninja consider what the Enemy and Food sprites’ scales should be set to. Prompt the ninja to think about whether they should be smaller than, larger than, or the same as each sprite’s original size. If the ninja is unfamiliar with decimals, explain the concept to them in thinking about whether the sprite should be displayed as half or a quarter of its original size and what number that converts to.
steps.instructions:
Add the Enemy and Food sprites’ locations to the minimap to track where they are on the tilemap!


Inside the onUpdate loop, copy the includeSprite function and paste it twice above the setImage function.


Update the sprite parameters in both functions so that both the Enemy and Food sprites are drawn on the minimap.


Click ▶ to use the minimap to collect the Food sprite, while avoiding the Enemy sprite!

steps.hints: ❓  Did you set the countdown timer to a challenging, but attainable number?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the countdown be set to so that the game is challenging, but not impossible?

❓ What directions might be helpful for the user at the beginning of the project? 

❓ What other User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) features might be added to this project? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider the UI/UX features that they’ve seen before and may already be familiar with (such as splash/game over screens, a choice menu, allowing the user to select their character, text that appears when a user interacts with something, etc.). Ask the ninja to consider how adding UI features to a project improves the User Experience (UX) of a game.
steps.instructions:
Add an extra challenge and instructions to the beginning of the project!


Add a // project start comment above // project events. Underneath, add code to start a countdown so that the Player sprite has a set amount of time to collect the Food sprite.


Then, add code to set the dialog frame to the frameImage asset and display instructions when the project begins.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Maps of all Sizes!
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses the Minimap extension to show a zoomed out display of the sprites and tilemap on screen!

validationItems.text: Create a minimap image of the project’s tilemap.
Add the minimap image to the project as a sprite.
Pin the minimap sprite to the top left corner of the screen.
Update the minimap image with the Player, Enemy, and Coin sprite locations as the project runs.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 10 of Brown Belt! Before you create your final Brown Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 10:

badges.title: Extension Explorer
badges.description: Use the minimap, status bar, timer, and raycasting extensions to enhance a project.

badges.title: Bird’s Eye View
badges.description: Create and pin a minimap displaying a smaller representation of sprites and the tilemap in a corner of the screen.

badges.title: Gauging the Action
badges.description: Make something happen based on the value of a status bar.

badges.title: Wait for the Signal
badges.description: Use throttle to delay an action in a game.

badges.title: Right on Cue
badges.description: Run a chunk of code after a certain amount of time has passed.

badges.title: In-Depth Image
badges.description: Create a 3D version of a tilemap from a sprite’s perspective.

badges.title: Points of View
badges.description: Toggle between 3D and top-down views of a tilemap.
